newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU steps up pressure on Japan over shipping.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU steps up pressure on Japan over shipping.

text.p: The European Union on Monday took steps to eliminate what it said were unfair Japanese harbour practices, formally calling for consultations under World Trade Organisation rules.
The European Commission -- the EU's executive -- said a monopoly on stevedore services by the Japanese Harbour Transportation Authority (JHTA) left European ship operators open to discrimination.
The Commission has zeroed in on red tape faced by shipping lines which wish at short notice to change the docking schedules of their vessels at Japanese ports.
A Commission official said loading and unloading "slots" were controlled entirely by the JHTA, which allocated stevedores to vessels on a rota basis.
In comparison, once a vessel was given a slot at a EU port, shipowners could negotiate with stevedores for the best rates, the Commission said.
The EU has called for consultations under Article VIII of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, which deals with fees and formalities connected with imports and exports of WTO member states.
Under WTO procedure, if Japan refuses consultations or no agreement is reached, the EU can press for a full panel to give a ruling on the matter.
Japan's harbour practices have long been a mystery to foreign shipowners and Japanese film makers have portrayed harbours as being controlled by the "Yakuza" or mafia.
Officials cite a practice under which Japanese stevedores charge $180 to compulsorily measure every container they handle -- despite the fact that container sizes are now standardized.
They say it also nearly impossible for ship owners to get a slot on a Sunday as Japanese unions have resisted a seven-day working week.

Although practices such as this are slowing being whittled away, Commission officials say they are concerned at a lack of transparency in the stevedore business and a lack of progress in pressing the Japanse government for change.

A Japanese diplomat, reacting to the Commission's move, said that his country believed that as the stevedore business was privately run, it had no say in the matter, but this has failed to satisfy the EU.
The Commission has taken the action under Article VIII in order not to include the issue in a wider global agreement on maritime services, negotiations for which stalled in June.

Talks on an agreement foundered when only 24 parties submitted conditional offers and the WTO has since been pressing for a resumption of talks with the hope of accelerating the process at the organisation's ministerial meeting in Singapore in December.

When maritime services negotiations collapsed in June, countries undertook to respect a "peace clause" in that they would not attempt to improve their current positions by imposing further restrictions.
